turn_text: The question with waters of the U.S. If it is eliminated, is it time to start work on clearer definitions for waters of the U.S. and clarity on
navigable waters?

First, let's just backtrack here a little bit to this review of why we're at. We go all the way back to 1972 when the EPA was created that that's the Clean Water Act, and that was meant to be a partnership between the states and the federal government where the states would implement and enforce Clean Water Act under the guidance of the USCP of the feds. And I think it's, you know, it's worked pretty good. We've gone a long ways, point source pollution. We've limited a lot of point source pollution. Nonpoint, we've made a lot of huge progress in nonpoint. I'm going to go back in the 60s, 70s, and then you know what nonpoint source pollution was. And not to say we still don't have to challenge you. I talk about Lake Erie if the algae problem. And, you know, you're using the Chesapeake Bay around the country. So there's still, there's still challenges out there. But when it comes to water quality, I think we've made good strides in working towards, you know, improving all the time. The problem with the rule that was proposed by the Obama administration in the waters of the United States was the result of two Supreme Court decisions, the swank and the promise decision back. in the mid-2000s. And the court, hard and fun here, kind of made the water a little bit because they didn't define navigable. And of course, when the Clean Water Act was passed in 1972, they put the word in the navigable. And they said, navigable waters will be under a more jurisdiction of the Clean Water Act than the U.S. EPA. And that was to go after the polluters of the 1960s and go after them with severe fines and even jail time, so the Clean Water Act. But they didn't define navigable. Now, you know, navigable to most people can go down the river. That's, I would say, navigable, it can do. You know, where's the stop? The Supreme Court decision said, well, they didn't define it either. And they left it open for waters that maybe it could affect what most people think navigable waters. And I think at a very important point to make here is some people believe that without this rule, they believe that waters that aren't navigable aren't being regulated. Well, I want to, you know, I'm sure the listeners here that that is not the case. All waters are being regulated and they might be regulated by the states if they're just, you know, little streams or road ditches or whatever. You know, I'm a former hog farmer. I couldn't go out and get something in my hog manure in the road ditch or whatever. That would be very common to us. So, but this idea, you know, this voter's rule had to happen because waters weren't being regulated. There's a fallacy. That's not the case. But what it does, it broadens the perspectives of the Clean Water Act and opens up very tough penalties that were actually meant by Congress at the time to go after the polluters. And so I think it's very important that the rule will be stopped. Unfortunately, the federal court in Cincinnati has put a hole on it. You know, I want to look at ways to address the Supreme Court decisions in a right, common sense manner. And so I'm looking at holding some round tables and doing some things with the stakeholders and get some input from the industry. And I guess my thought is, I think we need to address it because I think future administrations could bring it back up because they still have the basis of what the U.S. Supreme Court did in the Rapunzel Swank decision. So that's my fear that could be brought back up. Jeff, interesting too, we cannot do a congressional review act on this rule because it was passed at 60 legislative days.
